questions.q: The code that picks a payment provider by country is copied in the checkout, the refund handler and the webhook. What problem does a factory solve here?
questions.explain: The Kenyan refunds went to the wrong provider because one copy was not updated. With one factory, adding a country is one change that every caller sees.
options: It makes payments faster
It puts the knowledge "which provider, and how to build it" in one place, so the copies cannot drift apart
It removes the need for configuration
It lets you use inheritance instead of interfaces

questions.q: What should a provider factory do for a country it does not know?
questions.explain: A silent default is exactly how refunds ended up at Stripe. Unknown input is a configuration or programming error and should fail loudly and early.
options: Return a default provider so checkout keeps working
Return undefined and let the caller decide
Throw a clear error, and a startup check should build every configured country so the error appears at deploy time
Log a warning and use the first provider in the table

questions.q: A customer paid in Kenya through M-Pesa and later moved to Ghana. Which provider must refund them, and how does the code know?
questions.explain: Money can only be refunded by the provider that took it. Routing (country to provider) can change; the recorded provider of a past charge cannot.
options: Flutterwave, because refunds follow the customer's current country
M-Pesa, because the charge record stores the name of the provider that took the payment and the refund builds that provider
Whichever provider is cheapest
The default provider

questions.q: Why does the lesson keep routes (country to provider name) separate from builders (provider name to object)?
questions.explain: Changing the routing table affects new payments only. Refunds and webhooks look up the builder by the recorded provider name.
options: Because TypeScript cannot put functions and strings in one object
They are two different facts that change for different reasons; if Kenya moves to Flutterwave, old M-Pesa charges must still be refunded through M-Pesa
To make the code longer and easier to read
Because Record can only have string values

questions.q: Why are the factory's tables typed as Record<Country, ProviderName> instead of Record<string, ProviderName>?
questions.explain: The compiler becomes the checklist that the copied if chains never had. A Record<string, …> accepts any subset of keys.
options: It makes lookups faster
A Record over a union requires a key for every member, so adding a country to the union without a route is a compile error
It lets the table be changed at run time
It prevents the table from being exported

questions.q: What does building every routed provider once at application start achieve?
questions.explain: The compiler checks that the tables are complete; only running the factory checks that the environment actually has every secret key.
options: It warms up the providers' caches
A missing key or a broken route fails the deploy, instead of failing the first real customer's payment
It makes every provider a singleton
Nothing, the providers are built again later anyway

questions.q: When is a static factory method such as Money.fromNaira(12.5) better than a public constructor?
questions.explain: A named constructor says what its argument means and can refuse bad input before an object exists. A private constructor makes it the only door.
options: Never; constructors are always clearer
When construction must validate or convert, or when there are several ways to create the object that need clear names (fromNaira, fromKobo)
Only when the class has no fields
When you want a singleton

questions.q: A service calls createPaymentProvider(...) directly inside its methods. What is the problem, and the fix?
questions.explain: A factory hides which class, but calling it directly still fixes which factory. Receiving it as a dependency moves that choice to the composition root.
options: No problem; factories are always safe to call anywhere
The service is coupled to the real providers again, so tests move money. Inject the factory (makeProvider: (name) => PaymentProvider) so a test can pass one that builds fakes
The fix is to make the factory a singleton
The fix is to call new instead

questions.q: A factory reads process.env.PAYSTACK_KEY inside itself. Why does the lesson advise against this?
questions.explain: Pass configuration in, as createPaymentProvider(name, keys) does. The composition root reads the environment once.
options: Environment variables are slow to read
It is a hidden dependency on global state: tests cannot pass other keys without changing the process environment, and the signature does not show what the factory needs
Factories may not use strings
Because process does not exist in Node

questions.q: Staging used STORAGE=disk and QUEUE=redis. The worker on another machine could not find uploaded files. What kind of problem is this?
questions.explain: Each setting was valid alone; the combination was not. An abstract factory makes the family the unit of choice, so a mix cannot be configured.
options: A bug in the Redis client
Two parts that must come from the same family (single machine, or shared cloud) were configured independently and mixed
The worker is too slow
The files were too large

questions.q: What does an abstract factory give you that two separate factories do not?
questions.explain: localInfrastructure() returns disk storage and an in-process queue; cloudInfrastructure() returns shared storage and a shared queue. There is no way to ask for disk plus Redis.
options: Faster object creation
Picking one factory picks every part of a family together, so related parts always match
Inheritance between storage and queue
The ability to create objects without interfaces

questions.q: A project has one environment and one kind of storage and queue. Should it introduce an abstract factory now?
questions.explain: Patterns earn their place by solving a problem you have. With one family, the pattern adds names and indirection and hides nothing (YAGNI).
options: Yes, every project needs one
No. With one family there is nothing to mix; add it when a second family exists and mixing becomes a real risk
Yes, but only for tests
No, abstract factories are deprecated

questions.q: A function takes eight positional parameters and two of them were swapped in a call. What should you reach for first in TypeScript?
questions.explain: An options object fixes the swap with the least code. A builder is for step-by-step construction with rules, such as a query.
options: A builder class with one method per parameter
An options object with named properties, so each value is labelled at the call site
A singleton that stores the parameters
An abstract factory

questions.q: Which situation calls for a builder rather than an options object?
questions.explain: The query is built in steps, has rules that span steps (placeholder numbering), and is assembled at the end: exactly what a builder is for.
options: Creating a user with a name and an e-mail
Building a search query from any combination of optional filters, with numbered placeholders, validated limits and a final assembly step
Passing three booleans to a function
Reading a configuration file

questions.q: What is a fluent interface?
questions.explain: Fluent style is common for builders. Whether each method returns this or a new object is a separate choice, and it matters.
options: An interface with only optional properties
An API whose methods return an object you can call the next method on, so calls chain like a sentence: OrderQuery.all().status("paid").limit(10)
An interface that changes at run time
A TypeScript feature for async code

questions.q: Why does the lesson's OrderQuery return a new builder from every method instead of changing itself and returning this?
questions.explain: With a mutable builder, paid.where(a) and paid.where(b) change the same object, so both "derived" queries contain both filters.
options: Returning this is not allowed in TypeScript
So a partly built query can be shared: deriving two queries from one base query must not add each other's filters
New objects are faster
To make the builder a singleton

questions.q: Why does the query builder keep user input in values and put only $1, $2 in the SQL text?
questions.explain: Placeholders are how parameterised queries work. The builder's job is to make the safe way the easy way, including the placeholder numbering.
options: PostgreSQL requires every query to have at least one value
The database treats values as data, never as SQL, so input such as x' OR '1'='1 cannot change the query: no SQL injection
It makes the SQL shorter
It sorts the values

questions.q: sortBy(column: "placed_at" | "total_kobo", direction: "ASC" | "DESC") goes directly into the SQL text, not into values. Why is that safe?
questions.explain: Identifiers and keywords cannot be parameters. The union narrows them to known-safe literals in code; at run time, input from a URL must be validated against the same list first, since types do not exist at run time.
options: Because sort columns cannot be injected
Column names cannot be placeholders, so the builder only accepts a fixed set of values; any value from outside must be checked against that set before it reaches the builder
Because PostgreSQL escapes ORDER BY automatically
It is not safe at all

questions.q: Which two problems did the AppConfig.getInstance() singleton cause?
questions.explain: Tests became order-dependent because one test's setting stayed in the shared instance, and no test could hand the function a configuration of its own.
options: It was slow and used too much memory
A hidden dependency (the signature of maxQuantity() does not show it reads configuration) and global mutable state shared by every test
It could not be imported and could not be exported
It forced the use of inheritance and interfaces

questions.q: export const pool = createPool(process.env.DATABASE_URL) at the top of a module is also a singleton. What extra problem does it add?
questions.explain: ES modules are evaluated once and cached, so every importer shares the object, and the side effect happens as soon as anything imports it. Create it in the composition root instead.
options: Modules cannot export constants
The work runs at import time, so merely importing the file (for example in a unit test) reads the environment and opens connections
Each importer gets a different pool
It cannot be used with TypeScript

questions.q: What is the key difference between the singleton pattern and a singleton lifetime in a DI container?
questions.explain: "There is one of these" is a wiring decision. Made in the composition root, it is visible, and tests can make their own instance.
options: There is none
In the pattern the class decides and gives global access; with a lifetime the composition root or container decides, and users receive the instance as a dependency
The lifetime creates one instance per method call
The pattern supports tests better

questions.q: A singleton service stores currentUser in a field, set at the start of each request. What goes wrong under load?
questions.explain: Single-threaded does not mean one request at a time: requests interleave at every await. Per-request data needs a per-request (scoped) lifetime or explicit parameters.
options: Nothing, JavaScript is single-threaded
Two overlapping async requests share the one field, so one request can read the other user's identity after an await
The field is reset to undefined by the garbage collector
The service becomes transient

questions.q: With @zudojs/container, a factory registered with ContainerScope.SINGLETON runs how often?
questions.explain: That is what makes the container lifetime test-friendly: each test creates a fresh container and gets a fresh "singleton", with nothing shared with the application.
options: Once per process, no matter how many containers exist
Once per container: the first resolve builds it, later resolves return the same object, and a test's own container builds its own
On every resolve
Once per request

questions.q: The lesson's loadConfig returns Object.freeze({ ... }) and the one object is shared by the whole app. Why is this sharing harmless?
questions.explain: The singleton's problems come from shared mutable state and global access. Frozen and passed in, the configuration has neither.
options: Frozen objects are copied on every read
Shared immutable state cannot be changed by one user and observed by another, so it has none of the singleton's order-dependence
Freezing makes the object a singleton
Freezing hides the object from tests

questions.q: For test data, when does makeOrder({ status: "paid" }) (defaults plus a Partial of overrides) replace a full test data builder?
questions.explain: Test data builders shine when construction has steps or rules (.paid() also sets a charge id and paid date). For plain overrides, the function is simpler.
options: Never; tests always need builders
Usually: most tests only override a few fields, and one function with defaults does that with less code
Only when the order has no nested objects
Only in JavaScript, not TypeScript

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Every unknown value, including the lower-case "ng", silently falls to the default. A factory should throw for unknown input instead.
options: paystack mpesa paystack
paystack stripe stripe
paystack stripe paystack
An error for KE

questions.q: Why does the factory use Object.hasOwn? What does this print?
questions.explain: Plain objects inherit toString from Object.prototype. A lookup or an in check would treat "toString" as a known country. Object.hasOwn only accepts the table's own keys.
questions.code:
const routes: Record<string, string> = { NG: "paystack", GH: "flutterwave" };

console.log(typeof routes["toString"], "toString" in routes, Object.hasOwn(routes, "toString"));
options: undefined false false
function true false
function false false
string true true

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each call to the factory creates a new object with its own next counter (a closure). Whether callers should share one instance or get new ones is a lifetime decision.
options: MP-1 MP-2 MP-3
MP-1 MP-2 MP-1
MP-1 MP-1 MP-1
MP-1 MP-2 MP-2

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: where changes the builder and returns the same object, so base, big and ada are one object with all three filters.
options: paid+big false
paid+big+ada true
paid+big+ada false
paid+ada true

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each call copies the list and returns a new query, so the base stays as it was and each derived query has only its own extra filter.
options: paid+big+ada paid+big+ada paid+big+ada
paid paid+big paid+big+ada
paid paid+big paid+ada
paid+big paid+big paid+ada

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: PostgreSQL placeholders start at $1, so the index is shifted by one. `$${…}` is a literal dollar sign followed by an interpolation.
options: status = ? AND total_kobo >= ? AND email = ?
status = $0 AND total_kobo >= $1 AND email = $2
status = $1 AND total_kobo >= $2 AND email = $3
status = paid AND total_kobo >= 1000000 AND email = ada@shop.ng

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The same testDefault passes before testGhana runs and fails after it, because both use the one shared instance. The result depends on test order.
options: PASS PASS PASS
PASS PASS FAIL
FAIL PASS FAIL
PASS FAIL PASS

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Assigning to a frozen object's property throws a TypeError in strict-mode code (modules are strict), and the value stays 5. Shared and frozen is safe to share.
options: 99 true

false
99 true

true
5 true
5 false

questions.q: A tiny hand-written container supports two lifetimes. What does this print?
questions.explain: The singleton builds once (built = 1) and returns the same object. Each transient call builds a new object (built = 2, then 3), so they are not identical.
options: true true 2
true false 3
false false 4
true false 4

questions.explain: Each environment picks one family, so storage and queue always match. The loop visits cloud first because that is the order of the array.
options:
cloud: s3 + memory
local: disk + redis

cloud: s3 + redis
local: disk + memory

local: disk + memory

questions.q: Write createNotifier(channel): a factory that returns { send(to) } objects for "email" (returns "email to " + to) and "sms" (returns "sms to " + to), using a table typed as Record<Channel, …>. For any other string it must throw new Error("unknown channel: " + channel). The program should print sms to 0803 then unknown channel: fax.
questions.explain: One table knows every channel, the Record type keeps it complete when Channel grows, and unknown input fails loudly.

questions.q: Write startupCheck(routes, keys): for every country in routes, check that the routed provider has a non-empty key, and return a list of messages like "KE: missing key for mpesa". The program should print [ 'KE: missing key for mpesa' ].
questions.explain: Run at startup, this turns an empty secret into a failed deploy with a precise message, instead of a failed payment for the first Kenyan customer.

questions.q: Write a class Money with a private constructor, a readonly kobo field, and two static factory methods: fromKobo(n) (must be a safe integer) and fromNaira(n) (converts with Math.round(n * 100)). Both throw new Error("invalid amount") for negative or non-finite input. The program should print 1250 1250 then invalid amount.
questions.explain: The names say what the number means, and the private constructor makes these checked methods the only way to create a Money.

questions.q: Finish the immutable builder: where(sql, value) must return a new TaskQuery with the extra filter, and build() must number the placeholders $1, $2… The program should print SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE done = $1 AND owner = $2, then [ false, 'ada' ], then SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE done = $1.
questions.explain: Because where copies instead of mutating, the shared base query open keeps its single filter after Ada's query is derived from it.
questions.expected:
SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE done = $1 AND owner = $2
[ false, 'ada' ]
SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE done = $1

questions.q: Replace the positional parameters with an options object: createBooking({ guest, room, nights, breakfast }) where breakfast is optional and defaults to false. It returns "<guest>: room <room>, <nights> nights" plus ", breakfast" when chosen. The program should print Ngozi: room 204, 3 nights, breakfast then Musa: room 101, 1 nights.
questions.explain: Every value is named at the call site, so room and nights can no longer be swapped unnoticed, and the optional flag has a default. No builder needed.
questions.expected:
Ngozi: room 204, 3 nights, breakfast
Musa: room 101, 1 nights

questions.q: canOrder reads a global settings object. Change it to take the configuration as a second parameter, and run two "tests" that each pass their own frozen configuration. The program should print PASS twice.
questions.explain: The dependency is visible in the signature and each test controls its own configuration, so no test can leak settings into another.

questions.q: Write once(make), a singleton lifetime helper: it returns a function that calls make the first time and returns the same object on every later call. The program should print true 1.
questions.explain: This is what a container's singleton lifetime does per registration. The class being created knows nothing about it, and a test can call once again to get a fresh instance.

questions.q: Write testInfrastructure(log), a third family for the Infrastructure interface whose storage and queue record every call in log ("put uploads/1.jpg", "enqueue thumbnail uploads/1.jpg"). The program should print [ 'put uploads/1.jpg', 'enqueue thumbnail uploads/1.jpg' ].
questions.explain: A test environment is just one more family. upload did not change; the composition root of the test picked a different factory.
